newsitem.title: ROMANIA: ROMANIA PARLIAMENT IN UPROAR OVER CEAUSESCU PALACE.
newsitem.headline: ROMANIA PARLIAMENT IN UPROAR OVER CEAUSESCU PALACE.

text.p: Romania's parliament, now dominated by centrists, was embroiled in a row on Thursday on the eve of its first sitting over a decision to move into the grandiose palace built by executed dictator Nicolae Ceasescu.

Reformists backing President-elect Emil Constantinescu say they want nothing to do with the marble palace of more than 3,000 halls built on the banks of the River Dimbovita after Ceausescu demolished one-third of Bucharest city centre.

The leftist Party of Social Democracy (PDSR), thrown out of government in this month's general elections, backs the move to what Ceausescu called "The People's House". It says the current 19th-century building has been damaged by earthquakes.
The lower house, the chamber of deputies, is to sit in the palace on Friday ahead of Constantinescu's inauguration in a session expected to deal largely with procedural matters.
The Senate remains in the old building, once the Communist Party Central Committee headquarters, but is also due to move.

"The new parliament can reverse the decision to move into the palace, but it would be a pity," Adrian Nastase, outgoing PDSR chairman of the lower house, told journalists this week on a three-hour tour of the halls, some the size of soccer fields.
"This building is cold. It needs more life. We have to bring in works of art, rent or buy them."
He said refurbishing the palace for deputies had so far cost the equivalent of $32 million, all of which would be wasted if parliament changed its mind.
Ion Diaconescu, an ally of the president and head of the National Peasant Party tipped to replace Nastase, has repeatedly said the palace is too large and too expensive.
Newspapers quoted officials as saying annual upkeep of the lower house in the palace would soak up more than $500,000. Moving in the Senate would cost an additional $700,000.

Constantinescu, who defeated ex-communist Ion Iliescu last weekend, campaigned to speed reforms with a blend of financial discipline and benefits to help millions living in poverty since Ceausescu was executed in a bloody 1989 upheaval.

The president-elect made the fight against corruption and largesse a plank of his campaign and promised to cut budgets for protocol and ceremonies. He also vowed he would not move into the Cotroceni presidential residence near the city centre.
His prime minister-designate, Victor Ciorbea, has also said he will wage war on corruption as he did in a clear-out of city hall officials during a five-month tenure as Bucharest mayor.
Bucharest media have denounced Nastase's purchases of hundreds of thousands of dollars worth of silverware, crystal and leather furniture against the backdrop of mass poverty.

"Luxury that defies common sense," the daily Romania Libera said on Thursday. It listed some facilities at MPs' disposal -- a switchboard with 3,600 extensions, tennis courts and a club in two halls created for Ceausescu and his wife Elena.
Ceausescu did not live to inaugurate the 66,000 square metre (710,000 square feet) palace, its halls festooned with columns, endless inlaid marbled corridors and chandeliers.
The world's second largest building after the Pentagon in Washington, it was built by a workforce of 20,000, many of them conscripts, working in 12-hour shifts for five years.

Construction of the palace and of a broad fountain-lined avenue on the opposite bank of the river named "Boulevard of the Victory of Socialism" meant destruction of hundreds of century-old building and churches. REUTER
